That the House of Commons approves and supports in principle the diplomatic note defending Canadian rights and interests under the Boundary Waters Treaty in order to avoid the needless polluting of two major Canadian river systems.

I am sure that the people of Vancouver, and of British Columbia generally where much growth has taken place, are proud of the Rockies. I, as a citizen of Ontario, am proud of Ontario. As a citizen of Ontario, of course, I have the right to think that perhaps Ontario is the finest place in the world. On the other hand, my friends from Quebec, with the great natural resources of that province and the things they have done, may think their province is the best. For example, some of us have been critical of the fact that the Olympics will be held in Montreal. Let me tell hon. members that it took Quebecers and the mayor of Montreal to bring the Olympics to that city. I do not blame them for being proud of that fact.

More than that and more than the Maritimes, western Ontario, Quebec and so on, when the Great Architect of the universe created this earth, he put into Canada people who were willing to work hard. Our forefathers were not looking for a 35 or 40 hour week. They were not looking for an old age pension of $200 a month or $20 a month for each child. They were only looking for the opportunity to work hard. They certainly did work hard to make this country what it is. In so doing, they were happy.

If a person is unwilling to face that fact, there is something wrong with him. What would be the advantage of building a pipeline from western Canada to Montreal if we did not have any oil to ship through it? Where would the oil come from if it were not for the American dollars that were used to drill for the oil 10 or 15 years ago?
A couple of years ago I had the opportunity to visit Sept lies, Quebec. If I recall correctly, the wage earners of that community are the second highest paid in all of Canada. The people in Oakville are first. Twenty-five years ago there were perhaps six or seven shacks there. You could not really say anyone lived there. Today, Sept lies is one of the most modern cities in Canada. Over 20,000 people live there. It has one of the highest standards of living in the world. One American laid out the town and developed the two mines that are there. Every single dollar that was spent was an American dollar. Every single labourer who
November 21, 1973

worked on that project was a Canadian, except the man at the top. They paid 100 per cent Canadian taxes. If the Americans had not come, there would still only be six or seven shacks in Sept lies.

speechtext: There would be 50.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext:
That may be true. When I was a member of the Ontario legislature, I had the privilege of listening to a man whom I regard as the great Canadian, the Hon. Leslie Frost, who was then premier. He was speaking in an offhanded way. He said that in his opinion, there is not much difference between an American dollar bill and a Canadian dollar bill. He said if you go to the grocery store, you can buy just as many groceries with one as with the other. I will agree that things have certainly changed since the days of Leslie Frost.
There is no doubt that, as Canadians, we should have the control of our destiny and assets that are in Canada. On the other hand, we need the help and assistance of the United States and other foreign countries. We must be very thankful for the help we have received. I have the highest respect for my friends who are referred to as being "to the left" here in Canada. One thing is certain, they are sincere. They are sincerely wrong. Nevertheless, they are sincere and really believe that what they are doing is right.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) is a man whom I really appreciate. He is a devoted, honest politician. When he was honoured for the length of time he has been a member of the House of Commons, he mentioned that when he came here there was no old age pension or, if there was, it was $20 on a means test. Today, it is substantially higher. I am in favour of old age pensions. I believe in assisting people who need assistance. However, you can only have the social security programs the country can afford. Somewhere along the line you must stop. What worries me about the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre is now that the pension is $150 a month, he will want it to be increased to $200 a month. When it gets to $200 he will want it to go to $250. When it gets to $250, he will want $300.
I ask my socialistic friends, who made it possible to pay pensions at the level at which they now are? Who made it possible to give free medicare within reason across Canada? These things have been made possible through the development of this country by Canadian business and foreign business which invested here. It has been made possible by the individuals who pay the taxes. My friends to the left must remember that when pensions are increased substantially every year, the tax load goes up and up. They must remember that 85 per cent of the personal income tax that came from Canadians was paid by people who earned less than $15,000 a year.
In conclusion, I am glad this bill has been introduced by the minister. I have never really worried as long as foreign business interests have obeyed Canadian laws and hired Canadian labour. That is what is important. If this bill is not strong enough, and if we find the odd foreign enterprise which is not willing to do what we as legislators wish them to do, under our democratic system we can change the law so they will do what they should do for us as Canadian citizens.
Foreign Investment Review Act

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is always a pleasure to follow the hon. member for Bruce (Mr. Whicher). He used to sit across from me when the Liberals were in the position of having a rump on this side of the House. As one of my colleagues said, perhaps we converted him because there was much in his speech with which I personally agree.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext: He will be joining Paul Hellyer.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext:
With the different kind of rump we now have in the House, the NDP, I am sure the hon. member for Bruce will not sit there. While I am sure the hon. member for Bruce is happy about the concept embodied in this legislation, I believe that like many of us he would be happier still if the minister were not so intransigent and if he had been more agreeable to allowing for more consultation with the provinces. However, much has been said on this point and I do not wish to go over old ground. The hon. member for Bruce has reminded us of the wonderful nation in which we live. I think he would agree, though, that the traditional free enterprise system which has made Canada such a great country has been badly eroded in recent years, and I am sure he is a little concerned about the alliance between his party and those in the New Democratic Party who are so left wing they would make the late Salvador Allende look like Ronald Reagan. Even so, there are differences of opinion within that party and, indeed, no party is entirely undivided when expressing opinions on this subject of foreign investment.
It seems to me, as the hon. member for Cumberland-Colchester North (Mr. Coates) said yesterday, that during the period in which Liberal governments have been in control of the country, that is to say for 32 of the last 38 years, we have seen evidence of a deterioration in many aspects of our society. Perhaps this was to be expected. The present administration pays lip service to the idea of controlling foreign investment, but I am not at all confident that they are sincere in their promise of action to carry it out. Anyone who takes the trouble to look back in Hansard and refer to some of the promises which have been made by government spokesmen from time to time will understand the reason for this lack of confidence. I will cite just one example from the Hansard of March 14, 1972. The then minister of transport, now the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Jamieson), is reported as saying:
I agree with the claim that a reorganized structure is necessary in order that members and the country generally can obtain more information, and obtain it more easily, about all aspects of transportation. With this objective in mind, I propose to bring before the House in the next session three important pieces of legislation on which work is proceeding at the present time. The first of those is a bill designed to reconstitute Air Canada as a separate Crown corporation, thus divorcing it, as it were, from the CNR. I will also introduce a Canadian National Railways Revision Act and a companion piece of legislation covering amendments to the Railway Act. Hon. members will know how involved and far reaching these changes are; they have been asking for them for the last two or three years. These changes have entailed a great deal of work, which is still proceeding. I believe, however, that these bills are essential and I will bring them forward as soon as they are ready.
This is the type of thing the country and the House has grown to expect from the government opposite. I sincerely hope we shall not see an example of foot dragging in the

November 21, 1973
Foreign Investment Review Act case of the bill now before us, comparable to the example I have just cited. There are many other examples I might have used. Looking back on the record of the government during the last 32 out of 38 years, as far as examples of initiative and progressive action are concerned, and bearing in mind the situation today, I am bound to say I am reminded of the remark by Winston Churchill in his book "Great Contemporaries" when he said of Lord Roseberry: "He had outlived his past by 20 years and his future by 10." That comment could be directed with some justification toward the present administration, because it has been given no end of time in which to accomplish something.
Much has been made of the fact that in 1961 the Ottawa Valley Line was instituted to provide eastern Canadians with a source of oil other than western Canada. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald) said not long ago, that for years eastern consumers benefited from this decision. We have seen no essential change made in these arrangements, since 1961 though during the intervening years a man has been put on the moon and the economic condition of the entire world has changed. This government did not possess enough initiative to make any change in the policy set in 1961 as far as energy is concerned, although the situation changed.
To get back to the question of foreign investment in this country, I would again ask the minister to show a desire to be open, fair and frank in his administration of this legislation. In this way, those who have to deal with this policy would know in advance the criteria to be met. It is true the minister told us he would provide certain guidelines. He has told us that various circumstances would be taken into consideration. But once he has made a decision he is under no obligation to build up, as it were, any jurisprudence, or to give reasons for his decision. I believe he should keep this aspect in mind when administering the act; disclosure is necessary. I fail to see how this legislation can have its full impact unless Canadians are given an incentive to invest in their own country, to take a few risks and be rewarded for doing so. As long as tax anomalies exist which afford certain advantages to foreigners at the expense of Canadians, the type of legislation we are now considering will not be as advantageous as might otherwise be the case.
Like the hon. member for Bruce, I want to refer to another party in this House, the socialist party, the New Democratic Party to my left. It is interesting to listen to what some members of that party have to say, because in that party just as in my own, there is a considerable divergence of opinion. This applies not only to the particular piece of legislation we are now considering but to many other subjects as well. It is apparent to me that the NDP understands perfectly well some of the negative aspects of foreign investments. Speakers for that party have drawn attention to the fact, as, indeed, speakers from my party have done, that in some cases when a large consortium invests in Canada there are certain undesirable side effects. Sometimes a corporation tries to bring in its own employees and technicians. Sometimes it tries to make certain that much of the heavy equipment is supplied by firms with which these financiers have close ties.

A situation of this type is bad, and this legislation, as far as it tends to reverse it, is certainly good. The government, as many of us have stated, is to be commended for bringing the bill forward at this time. We are not denigrating hon. gentlemen opposite for bringing it forward. We think it is a constructive step, possibly one of the few constructive steps hon. gentlemen opposite have taken.

speechtext: Don't get political.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext: I see the parliamentary secretary partly agrees. I say to him: Go a little further. Let him seek to persuade some of the policy-makers in the cabinet to give a tax break to Canadians who are running family businesses, to Canadians who are in business in a small way.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext: We did.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext:
Well, the government has not gone far enough. It is not sufficient to adopt a negative approach and curtail foreign investment unless one is prepared to encourage Canadians to pick up the slack and take the risks which must be taken if this country is to be developed. A capital gains tax has been introduced. This is a fact of life. Although many people on the extreme right politically were against this tax, I felt it was time a capital gains tax of some kind was enacted. But in our tax law no consideration has been given to the position of the investor who sets aside money systematically over the years, and invests it over the years, for the purpose of building up a fund for the education of his children. No consideration is given to this investor when he sells his securities. He is hit with the same kind of capital gains tax as the wealthy speculator who cleans up on the Toronto stock exchange and makes $20,000 in six months. This is wrong.
There are many other modifications that the government must make in taxation policy. Kicking and screaming, they finally agreed that they were wrong about taxing family farms and corrected the situation; I commend them for that. But I say with all sincerity that they have to go a lot further than that if they want to promote Canadian nationalism and encourage Canadians by giving them a break, in so far as taxes are concerned.
The New Democratic Party recognizes the problems that are implicit in foreign ownership, but they are very negativistic, if I may use that word, in looking at the corollary to which I have referred. They do not concede, for example, that the provinces need to be consulted, as we have suggested should be provided for in this legislation. At least, if they do, then they have not shown that to be the case. I suggest that the New Democratic Party has certain members who are very uncomfortable, as are some of us, about some of the provisions in this bill.
Just so that I will not be accused of making idle references, I had occasion not too long ago to refer to an interesting speech made by the hon. member for Waterloo-Cambridge (Mr. Saltsman) on a different issue, unemployment insurance. I have always admired my hon. friend from Waterloo-Cambridge, and I realize that in many ways he is probably an ideological prisoner of the NDP. I should like the House to listen to what he said about unemployment insurance, which is one of the "holiest of
November 21, 1973

holiests" as far as socialists are concerned. As reported at page 5892 of Hansard for July 23 last he said:
What is the point in fishermen being included under the provisions of the act?
He advocates taking fishermen off unemployment insurance, apparently, because he goes on to say this:
Insurance is supposed to take care of unpredictable hazards. What is unpredictable about fishermen being unemployed?
I will not comment on that observation; I merely use it as an illustration that certain members of the New Democratic Party have strong opinions. It makes me chuckle when I hear them in this House day after day taking the sanctimonious approach that everything they propose is an example of, shall I say, complete and utter unanimity within their party. The other day the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) proposed an amendment, but his party did not support him on it. Nothing much has been said about that, though it is of interest that when that sort of thing happens to the Conservative party, where there is a little more freedom to be individuals, the NDP, attempt to make a great deal of capital out of it.
It is also very interesting, when talking of the members of the NDP, to examine some of the comments made recently regarding some other contradictions in their official policy. I have in mind a very interesting article by a journalist named John Nichol, in which some of the NDP economic theories were attacked. The hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broadbent) in a speech not too long ago in this chamber made mention of various provinces and took issue with some provincial administrations, their history and background. This particular article, which I am prepared to table if you wish, Mr. Speaker, goes on to say, in part:
Headline: Looking for hard cold cash?
Picture: Cash register with its drawer open.
Text: Come and get it!
You'll have to put it to use by locating within this province. But it'll be worth it. Look at the facts. Resources, labour force, markets-East, West and South, all at your fingertips.
If you're in manufacturing or processing industry looking to expand .. . take a hard look at Saskatchewan. If you qualify, we can help you greatly.
How much in hard cold cash? Write us. We'll come to you.
This advertisement was placed by the deputy minister of the department of industry and commerce of the province of Saskatchewan, the Saskatchewan Power Building, Regina, Saskatchewan. The article points out:
This conflicts directly with the views of the national NDP leader David Lewis.
I do not want to read this fairly lengthy article into the record in its entirety, but it goes on to say this:
The campaign of the NDP in the recent election campaign was one of very narrow focus. The only spokesman who got any attention was David Lewis, and he confined himself to his themes of "corporate rip-offs" and "corporate welfare bums" and the "phony incentive society".
Then, Mr. Nichol has this to say:
It is important to note that there are many dedicated supporters of the NDP who do not support Mr. Lewis on this issue.
I mention this not to be unkind to the leader of the New Democratic Party, a very able parliamentarian but one who, I think, sometimes degenerates into some sort of
Foreign Investment Review Act parliamentary "Pushme-Pullion" of Dr. Doolittle fame. He is pushing here, pulling there, all the time with great vigour, supposedly trying to topple the government, huffing and puffing but being completely ineffective and manifestly insincere. What John Nichol is pointing out is this:
The Manitoba Development Corporation, a Crown agency of Premier Schreyer's NDP government, loans tens of millions of dollars a year to private enterprise.
In short, these NDP supporters accept the fact that industrial incentives are an essential tool of government in desperately important tasks of finding jobs.
The premiers and the officials of the Canadian Labour Congress have active responsibilities for jobs. David Lewis does not. Therein lies the difference.
Looking once again at the ramifications and implications of this particular piece of legislation, just as the hon. member for Bruce indicated he was proud, so I too am very proud of being a Canadian. Indeed, I am sure all hon. members of this House are. We have a great deal of respect for the efforts that our forefathers made in building this nation. They did it, as the hon. member pointed out, with hard work and they were not unduly concerned with socialist doctrine. A lot of people from socialist countries who have voted with their feet, as the saying is, by crossing the border have come to Canada because they feel they have a chance under a free enterprise system. When I hear New Democratic Party members denigrating private enterprise, saying it has not done what it should and that the only answer is some magical solution to be found in socialism, I sometimes think that my hon. friends opposite on the government benches must be very uneasy indeed about associating themselves with such remarks and acceding to some of the policies to which they have been forced to accede in order to retain their precarious hold on power.
The day will come, Mr. Speaker, when there will be a reckoning. I have no doubt that in the not too distant future some of the provisions of this particular bill will be modified. They will be modified by a Progressive Conservative government. Hopefully, they will be modified before some of the more obscure and bureaucratically oriented provisions have damaged the economic climate in Canada to a very great extent.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to begin by making a few comments on the speeches of the two members who have preceded me. The hon. member for Bruce (Mr. Whicher) spoke for some 20 minutes, and it was not until the last minute of his speech that he said he was going to support this bill. The whole tenor of his remarks was a defence of the greatness of the free enterprise system, a defence that led me to believe he felt that the free enterprise system was so effective in meeting the needs of the people of Canada that we really had no need for the kind of legislation that his minister introduced and which the members of this party are going to support. However, the reason the hon. member for Bruce is going to support a bill which he spent 99 per cent of his time criticizing by implication I will leave the hon. member for Bruce to explain.
I want to say a few words about the speech made by the hon. member for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay) who has just taken his seat. It was a speech that I could listen to with a

November 21, 1973
Foreign Investment Review Act good deal more comfort than I could yesterday when I heard the speech made by another Conservative member, the hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Horner). If the hon. member for Central Nova does not agree with members of the New Democratic Party that does not surprise me. If he did agree he would be over here as a New Democrat, and if we agreed with him we would be sitting somewhere near him, but certainly not near the hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Horner).
There is one thing the hon. member said to which I want to take sharp objection. If I misunderstood him I apologize in advance. He said that many people in Canada had showed what they thought of socialism by leaving socialist countries. If the hon. member for Central Nova implied that the people who came to Canada from communist countries because they did not like their systems felt there was any resemblance between the systems of those countries and the NDP and its policies, I reject that out of hand. If the hon. member did not imply that, then what I have said does not apply to his speech.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext: What do you stand for then?

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext:
The NDP is associated formally and informally with the Labour Party of Great Britain, which has been and will be again the government of that country; it is associated with the Social Democratic Party of Sweden, which has been the government of that country for 40 years; it is associated with the Labour government of Norway, and that party has formed the government of that country for the better part of the last 30 years, and it is associated with the Social Democratic Party of the government of Willie Brant of West Germany. Those are the parties with which we are associated both in philosophy and through membership in the Socialist International. If the hon. member for Central Nova or any other member wants to criticize our position on this or on any other question they are welcome to do so. This is a democratic country and we are prepared to let the people of Canada, by their votes and in other ways, show what they think of our position. I want to say in the strongest terms that any suggestion by any hon. member of this House that our program has anything to do with or anything in common with countries in the communist world is simply not true, is unfair and a completely unfounded allegation.
We are discussing a bill which we hope, for the first time, will permit Canada to deal with one of the most important problems faced not only by this country but by every country in the western world. We have often heard it said here in the House and outside that we ought to look for examples of a country which has had the finest growth record since the end of World War II, and I suggest that country is Japan. For years now Japan has had legislation which requires that no foreign firm shall own more than 50 per cent of the company in Japan in which it has invested. This legislation was adopted years ago. It is not surprising then that we are for the first time beginning to think about what can be done in this country regarding foreign control.
The huge corporations of the world are, year by year, becoming bigger. The annual output of the 300 leading

multinational, transnational, or whatever you want to call them, companies which are today doing $300 billion worth of business a year will by 1990, if their present rate of expansion continues, be doing $2,000 billion worth of business. They will be responsible for 50 per cent of the gross national product of the free world. Those companies do not really produce and sell in the countries in which their factories happen to be located, their mines, their wells and other things. They set up branches and subsidiaries in other countries, import and export between each other and decide where they will get their raw materials and where they will produce their finished goods.
The hon. member for Bruce talked about visiting Sept lies and referred to how prosperous a city it was. I suggest that Sept lies is the port through which the iron ore taken out of northern Quebec and Labrador is shipped. There are some 10,000 miners digging iron ore in Quebec and Labrador. They are getting good wages, but that iron ore is shipped to Sept lies and most of it is exported to the United States where probably 200,000 U.S. workers are getting very good wages turning that iron ore into finished steel as well as processing that steel into manufactured goods such as cars, refrigerators, you name it, which are then sold in the United States, in Canada and in other countries. I suggest those workers in the United States are reaping the benefits of that iron ore, not the Canadian workers in Sept lies or in the iron ore mines of Quebec and Labrador.
In an article which appeared in the Toronto Star sometime ago Walter Stewart referred to the question of who makes the decisions in these multinational corporations. He quotes from the head of a British owned multinational corporation as follows:
"There is no such thing as a multinational firm. We have plants in half a dozen countries, trade in dozens more, but if you want to know who runs us, look where the control is-in London. That's where the budgets are approved, that's where the policies are laid down."
We should not be critical of the multinational corporations. They operate under the laws we have passed, and if we have failed to pass laws which assure that multinational corporations operate in the interests of the Canadian people rather than in the interests of their shareholders then we are at fault, not those corporations. Their objective, and it is legitimate from their point of view, is to make more money. The important thing is how they can make more money, where is the best place to provide jobs and where is the best place to locate their major plants? The answers to these questions in most cases are very simple. For political and economic reasons, the best places are not in Canada but in the country in which these companies have their head offices, where the real decisions are made. In most cases as far as Canada is concerned that is the United States.
It may be that because of the current crisis in the energy field resulting from decisions of the Arab states to cut back on the production and export of oil there will be a precipitous slowdown in economic activity, and I certainly hope that is not the case. However, when times are difficult, United States owned firms naturally tend to keep U.S. plants open at the expense of plants located in Canada. This has already happened in respect of certain industries. Westinghouse, for example, closed a plant in
November 21, 1973

London, and General Electric shifted its purchasing of T.V. tubes from Toronto to a plant in Japan. One could go on and on with examples, but this is the reason Canadians are concerned about foreign ownership.
This government has dithered and "dothered" about this for years. First, it had a study made under the former minister, Mr. Gordon, headed by Professor Watkins of the University of Toronto. Then, there was another study which they attempted to hide and which was finally made public. This was done under the present Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Gray). Then, last year a bill was brought in which did not begin to deal with the question. It was not proceeded with because we indicated very strongly that we would not support it. This is why we now have a bill which will give the government an opportunity to begin to deal with the question. There are many things which we believe should be contained in the bill which are not included. In earlier discussions we have suggested things which we believe should be included in the bill which are not. Some amendments and some improvements have been made, and because of this we will support the bill.
I want to say to the minister that we are very skeptical. In such a situation, the Americans would say they were from Missouri. I do not know what the Canadian equivalent is to being from Missouri.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext: Manitoba.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext:
My colleague the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) says the Canadian equivalent is Manitoba. I can accept that as a Manitoban. However, I should like to say we are very skeptical about the real intentions of this government and this minister. One can have the best legislation in the world, but if a government does not want to use it and does not want to enforce it, then the legislation will not be much used. One could not have a better illustration than the fact that for almost 50 years anti-combines legislation has been on the statute books, and for 50 years nothing effective has been done to control the ever-growing power of monopolies in Canada, to disperse or break them up.
So, I say to the minister that, of course the first step in doing anything about this question is the passage of legislation. The second step, however, about which we are skeptical and in respect of which we will be watching very carefully the performance of the government, and particularly of the minister, is the use of the legislation when enacted, to police the situation and to do whatever can be done to ensure that the continued takeover of Canadian industry by multinational corporations be, if not halted, at least slowed down.
Let me point out to members of the House that the extent of control of foreign corporations in this country is fantastic. It is of an order which has not been duplicated in any other country in the western world. Over 90 per cent of the oil and gas resources in this country are foreign owned. Over 80 per cent of the mining resources are foreign controlled. I think over 60 per cent of the manufacturing industries are foreign controlled. The percentage of that control has been accelerating rather than slowing
Foreign Investment Review Act down. According to Statistics Canada, in 1970 the last year for which it had figures, foreign investment in Canada increased by a record $2 billion. United States firms account for $1.6 billion of that $2 billion increase in 1970. Their total holdings amount to $21.5 billion, a 7.7 per cent increase over their interest in 1969. That is what foreign control means.
I suppose one of the worst examples to indicate that we cannot afford to manage this country without foreign investment is in the speeches of the hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Horner). The speech he made yesterday was by its nature a classic example of the type of speech he makes. It is the kind of argument which, if not endorsed by all members of the Conservative Party, seems to be supported certainly by every member of parliament from Alberta, everyone of whom, of course, is a Conservative. The hon. member for Crowfoot heaped scorn on us. According to him public ownership does not work. We believe in public ownership. He suggested that without private capital there would be no oil industry, no expansion and so on.
I wish to deal for a few moments with the illustration he used, the industry he used, as his clinching argument to show the fallacies in respect of public ownership and the fallacies concerning the position taken by the New Democratic Party. It is interesting to look at what has happened to the oil industry worldwide in recent years. I am sure I do not have to tell members of parliament what has happened in the countries which own the overwhelming majority of the proven oil reserves in the world. In virtually every country in the Middle East the situation has changed fantastically in recent years. From a time when the multinational oil corporations, such as Exxon, Shell and Gulf, owned the oil and paid a small royalty to the countries in which they extracted the oil, you have a situation now where in many cases the countries themselves have taken over and now own the producing oil wells. They have made arrangements with the multinational corporations to market the oil and so on but they now own it.
In other countries there has been a takeover to the extent of joint ownership, ownership on a 60-40 basis and so on, but increasingly the oil producing countries with the largest oil resources own the oil themselves or in partnership with private enterprise. The day when private enterprise was given free and exclusive rights to develop the oil resources in those countries is gone. What about the western world? In Great Britain, the largest company I believe is the British Petroleum Corporation. BP is almost 50 per cent owned by the British government. I am not sure whether that share of BP was acquired while the Labour Party formed the government or while the Conservative Party was in power. The Conservatives have been in office now for several years, and to my knowledge there has been and is no proposal that the state divest itself of its share. In France, the French government has a 35 per cent interest in CFP which is the eighth largest integrated oil company in the world. It also has a 100 per cent interest in the ELP oil company which was set up to exploit the crude oil deposits in those areas which operate with the French franc as their monetary standard.

The Italian government owns 100 per cent of the only oil corporation in the country, ENI, and incidentally it is the largest national oil company in the world, operating in Italy and many other countries. I have completely excluded countries which are communist controlled, and I give these illustrations simply to prove that more and more countries in the western world are finding it to the advantage of their people to have the state involved in the oil business and energy business. That is precisely what we have been advocating here.
Let me turn to the other point which was made so effectively last night by the hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Horner), and I mean effectively if one thinks in terms of making a case for the oil companies. As I listened to the hon. member I was sorry I did not have a bucket with me to catch the tears which poured from his eyes as he told us about the plight of the poor, defenceless oil companies if the rights which we have given them to find oil in this country, to own oil, to sell oil at current prices, were not continued. He told us also that if they were not allowed to increase their prices, they would be bankrupt tomorrow. Somebody has to answer that kind of argument put forward by the hon. member for Crowfoot. As I say, it was an extremely effective argument if one were only interested in the welfare of the oil companies. I want to put the facts on the record about the poor oil companies which, to listen to the hon. member for Crowfoot, are virtually going bankrupt. Let me take just three of those companies.
Gulf Oil in the five years from 1968 to 1972 in round figures made profits of $522 million. That is over $100 million each year. In deferred taxes, that is, taxes which it did not have to pay because of the kind of encouragement which governments have been persuaded oil companies need if they are to do business in Canada, to look for oil, and so forth, from 1968 to 1972 Gulf got over $109 million. Its actual profits for those years, and by actual profits I am talking about net income plus deferred taxes, were over $588 million. If you look at the return to the shareholders, which is shown as a percentage of net income, you see that between 1969 and 1972 that income was never less than 6.9 per cent in any year, and went up to a high of 8.7 per cent in 1972. If you include the deferred taxes as part of their earnings, their earnings for 1972 were 11.1 per cent. Need I tell hon. members of the House that because of increases in prices and increased use of oil, profits of the oil companies for the first nine months of 1973 are running at somewhere between 30 per cent and 40 per cent higher than they were in 1972?
Let me now turn to Shell Oil, another one of the companies about which I presume the hon. member for Crowfoot is concerned. In the ten years from 1962 to 1972, Shell Oil had a net income of $478 million. Its net income in 1972 was $79 million, an increase of 27 per cent over 1970 and, as I say, this year its profits are up probably by another 30 per cent. In 1971, Shell Canada had deferred taxes of over $8V2 million, and in 1972 its deferred taxes were over $10 million. Its actual profits with deferred taxes in 1971 were just under $71 million, and in 1972 they were over $89 million. The return on shareholders' investment capital in 1972 was 10.4 per cent. That is a pretty good profit for any

shareholder. I am not saying there is anything illegal or improper from their point of view. They are interested, and so they should be, in making as large profits as possible.
Now, what about the giant, the largest company- Imperial Oil? Between 1963 and 1972, Imperial Oil made $1,010 million in profits after taxes. In 1972, its profits were $151 million, an increase of 11 per cent over 1971. In 1971, its profits were $136 million, an increase of 29V2 per cent over the previous year. So far in 1973, its profits are running in the neighbourhood of 35 per cent more than they were in 1972. But, Mr. Speaker, that was not enough. In 1971, Imperial Oil was able to defer payment of taxes to the amount of $11 million, and in 1972 was able to defer payment of taxes to the amount of $26 million. Is it any wonder that members of this party cannot feel very sorry for the oil companies? They are doing very well for themselves, Mr. Speaker. If you look at the return on equity to the shareholders in percentage terms, through the years 1963 to 1972 you see that Imperial Oil never made less than 9.7 per cent, and in 1972 the return was 13.9 per cent. These were unconscionable profits.
This country faces an oil shortage in the maritime provinces and in Quebec. Why is that? It is not because of a shortage of oil. We have more than enough oil in western Canada to meet the needs of the eastern provinces. But we cannot supply those needs because there is no oil pipeline to carry the crude oil from Sarnia to Montreal. Why is there no such oil pipeline? The reason is simple. In 1961, the then Conservative government decided that the best way to meet the oil needs of the people of Canada was to adopt a policy under which oil for Nova Scotia, Newfoundland, New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island and Quebec would be supplied by imports from Venezuela and the Arab states, and that the rest of Canada from the Ottawa River west would be supplied with oil from Alberta sources. Mr. Speaker, until this year crude laid down in Montreal and purchased from Venezuela or the Arab states was cheaper than crude shipped from the west, so that is what the user got. The price of oil west of the Ottawa River was set by the oil companies in Alberta and that was what the consumer had to pay, even though it would have been cheaper to bring oil from Venezuela into Toronto. The Toronto-Hamilton-Ottawa user had to use western oil.
The price of oil has gone up now, and I do not blame the Venezuelan government for that. They are going to charge what the traffic will bear, but the eastern user is going to have to pay more. Had we built a pipeline, as members of this party and representatives of the independent oil producers have been recommending for years, western oil could now be shipped to Montreal to meet the needs of the eastern user. But that did not suit the western oil producers who had set the price so that they could make high profits. It did not suit them to have that pipeline built and former Conservative and Liberal governments went along with that.
It is not bad enough that homes and industries in the eastern provinces are going to have to pay more for oil because they have to pay the price which the Venezuelans and Arab countries want, but it is now proposed by the oil

Mr. Speaker, before beginning my main remarks I wish to refer to the closing of the debation the report stage on Monday evening. As Your Honour is aware, I had an amendment to this bill which was listed last on the order paper. At six o'clock that day the Acting Speaker, then the hon. member for Beauharnois-Salaberry (Mr. Laniel) suggested that it might possibly be out of order. As it was six o'clock, he suggested that perhaps comments could be made on the matter.
At the time I was unfortunately absent in Alberta, attending the funeral of our late colleague, Harry Kuntz. I only regret that the hon. member for Saint John-Lancas-ster (Mr. Bell) and the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Hellyer) were in such a mood at that time that they felt this bill needed very speedy passage. I felt that the acting speaker at the time could have chosen some better precedent for ruling my amendment out of order. I believe His Honour expressed the feeling that the amendment interfered with the legislative procedure which we have grown accustomed to in this country. I am not saying my amendment was completely in order; I would not have been surprised if it had been ruled out of order. However, I should not like to see that ruling, which did not evoke any response, to become the precedent for future rulings on amendments of that kind.
It seems to me that the legislative procedure has been adopted whereby we allow the provinces to accept or reject federal legislation in many areas. As an example, I can think of the Criminal Code, which allows provinces to hold lotteries or not hold them, as they will; I think of the Canada Pension Plan, under which we require provincial consent if the plan is to operate; I think of the medicare legislation, which a lot of provinces did not accept immediately. We needed the club of the federal spending power to bring them into line and participate in that federal legislation.
In 1964-65, this House passed special legislation setting up a procedure for allowing provinces to opt out of what is primarily national legislation. So, I do not know whether the ruling was well founded; however, I want to point out to the House that it was not-

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to make it perfectly clear that I am in no way critical of the hon. member who was Acting Speaker at that time, because he was the one who invited comments. I am complaining of hon. members of this House who failed, in my view, to live 
up to their duty and give him some assistance. That is the point.
The hon. member for Don Valley (Mr. Gillies) said, when speaking on this bill at the report stage, that in his opinion this is the most important piece of legislation the present parliament has so far considered. I agree. This legislation will have far reaching effects on the economic and social life of this country. I do not apologize for the time I shall take in dealing with it. Perhaps I will use my 40 minutes; perhaps I will not. I will do my best to cover the situation, and I apologize in advance if some of my remarks appear somewhat disjointed. As has been pointed out, this bill will have far reaching effects. It will be of concern to every part of the country and therefore deserves full and complete discussion.
The hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis) suggested that Canadians are concerned about foreign investment in Canada. I suppose he meets more people than I meet in his perambulations around the country. I think all members do a fair amount of travelling and talk to many people. I must say I have not noticed any burning concern across this country about foreign investment. Perhaps there is a burning concern in a certain select, elite group in Toronto, concentrated probably most heavily in the editorial rooms of the Toronto Star. I know that Hon. Walter Gordon has had certain ideas on this question for a long time. I suppose he is using his influence with the Toronto Star, and of course he has some influence. I suggest that the main thrust behind this legislation comes from there. Of course, the Toronto Star influences commentators, newscasters of the CBC, and others. The main news gathering and public opinion promoting facilities of the corporation are based in Toronto. That city is also the headquarters of the Canadian television network, of Maclean's magazine and of other great makers of Canadian public opinion. I suppose, as a result of cross-fertilization among these entities, there is now a strong pressure for controls over foreign investment in Canada.
We did not hear too much on this subject from that area when investment was needed to make it what it is now. People like Eddie Goodman of Cadillac Development Corporation-many call him Fast Eddie-support this type of legislation. Let me say that the system which allowed Fast Eddie to arrive where he is today could work well in other parts of the country. Mr. Goodman and his friends are not offering any of their profits for the development of, say, the Atlantic shelf, that is, for the development of energy in that region. I do not know how great a risk he and his friends would be prepared to take in investing profits, derived in large measure from the activities of people who have utilized money from outside Canada, in the development of that particular area.
I want to spend most of my time trying to relate this legislation to the energy field. As a member from Alberta, I am probably most acquainted with the relationship of this legislation to that particular field of endeavour. I was surprised to hear the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) so blatantly state the facts when referring to the problem of the great oil companies. However, it is important to note that the facts should be set out in a little different way.
November 21, 1973

I wish to refer to a story that appeared in the infamous newspaper the Toronto Star on November 14 under the heading "Imperial Oil tells employees its profits are not excessive". I quote:
In the current oil crisis, gasoline prices have been going up. Are the oil producers getting a larger share?
No, contends J. A. Armstrong, president of U.S.-controlled Imperial Oil Ltd.
Here's how he puts the company's position in a report to employees: "On the average the price Imperial receives for gasoline-the wholesale price at which the company sells it to the dealer, exclusive of federal and provincial taxes-has increased 21 per cent since 1948. In the same period . .. average weekly wages and salaries have increased by almost 400 per cent.
That does not sound like gouging.
"To put it another way. In 1948 the Canadian wage earner had to work 25 minutes to buy a gallon of gasoline. Today, he works eight minutes and today's gasoline is vastly superior to the product he bought in 1948."
Armstrong concedes that Imperial's profit has been increasing and has drawn some criticism. He mentions the high cost of exploration-$23 million spent by the industry during 30 years of exploration-
I question that. I think the reporter or typesetter left a zero off that figure. That should probably be an annual figure rather than the figure for 30 years. I am sorry, Mr. Speaker. I should have read a little further ahead.
-$23 million spent by the industry during 30 years of exploration in the Prairie provinces before discovery of the Leduc field in 1947 and $300 million risked in searching for oil on the Atlantic shelf since 1960.
We all know there has not been a find of commercial quality off the Atlantic shelf in that period.
"The Canadian oil industry made an after-tax profit in 1972 of 7.4 per cent on the money it used in its business. The after-tax profit in manufacturing generally that year was 7.3 per cent- essentially the same return in an industry that, by normal standards, is considered to face less risk."
Imperial last year had a profit of $151 million but, says Armstrong, these figures "tell nothing about the size of the investment on which it is based."
"A more meaningful way to look at a company's profit is in terms of how much it earned in total revenue. In 1972, Imperial's profit on each dollar was 7.3 per cent, which is just about the company's average of the past 25 years."
We have to realize that much capital is required in the resource industry. It is certainly a risky business, as I will attempt to show later. As indicated in Mr. Armstrong's statement, $300 million has been spent in the last 13 years off the east coast of Canada without a commercial find. We will not get people to put up that kind of money unless there is some hope for a better return if and when something is found. It is not the same as making widgets in Montreal because if that does not work, the company can go into something else. There is not the same risk over a long period of time.
Reference was made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North to other countries. He mentioned British Petroleum, a company in France and an Italian company. It should be pointed out that none of those companies were formed for operations within the territorial boundaries of those countries. British Petroleum was formed under the auspices of the late Sir Winston Churchill when he was First Lord of
Foreign Investment Review Act the Admiralty prior to World War I. He realized Britain needed a secure source of fuel for its navy. He felt it necessary to have a company in which the government had an interest in order to ensure national security. Since that time there has not been any operation by that company within the territorial limits of Great Britain, except possibly in the North Sea where a great number of companies are operating. The North Sea has certainly not been closed to foreign companies.
We now find more Canadian companies changing the emphasis of their exploration from Canada to the North Sea, yet the NDP say that we have a situation in Canada where there is no risk. They say there is no need to worry, you can drill anywhere and find anything you want. If that is so, why is interest being lost in Canadian operations? Why are exploration companies moving from Canada to the North Sea and the American Gulf coast? It is primarily because they do not know what the climate will be here. They do not know whether restrictions will be placed on future access to foreign money markets or whether the federal government will have policies to artificially keep the price down. They do not know whether there will be a change in the tax policy, the competition act or any number of things that are making the people engaged in that industry pull out their hair.
There is too much concern about the financial side. We have to look at the human side of the problem. After all, these Canadian companies employ Canadians, as do the foreign-controlled companies. Canada has developed a large body of scientifically trained personnel who are engaged in this industry. If the present situation continues much longer, we will lose them. The minister said yesterday that this legislation is necessary in order to get Canadians involved. I can say that in the energy industry we have an indigenous group of research people and highly qualified technicians who are liable to disappear if the policies of this government and its socialist friends are followed much longer.
I do not think members realize what the energy industry does for employment in this country. I wish to put some facts on the record. For every oil or gas well drilled, there are 16 people employed directly on the rig as well as two employees from a testing company, two employees of a logging company, two from a coring company, one welder, four camp caterers, two mud suppliers, two cementing company employees, two casing company employees, two bit supplier employees, three employees of the fuel dealer who supplies the fuel for the operations of the rig, three water haulers, eight employees of a trucking company, three rathole-conductor contractor employees and three lease construction employees. There are two surveyors as well as between 15 and 25 people employed in electrical, plumbing, hardware, rental, grocery, fishing and other occupations. For every oil drilling rig, between 70 and 80 people are employed.
I have listened to Eric Kierans. As far as he is concerned, the oil and gas industry does not employ anybody. It does not really deal with labour at all. Well, why is it that the unemployment rate in Alberta and Saskatchewan has been lower over the past number of years than in any other part of the country? Why is it difficult to find people

November 21, 1973
Foreign Investment Review Act to take jobs available in those areas if it is not because of the operations of the oil companies? In addition, the oil drilling industry is a totally Canadian industry. It is 95 per cent Canadian owned. Granted, it depends on two types of customers-oil companies which are not Canadian controlled, and oil companies which are. But this drilling industry, which employs a vast number of people, is 95 per cent Canadian owned and controlled. We do not always keep these things in mind. It seems to me we are sometimes so concerned about controlling foreign investment that we ignore some of the human consequences which may follow when some of these bureaucrats start fiddling around, as bureaucrats are apt to do, unsupervised by someone who has the interest of the whole country at heart.
The minister turned down every effort to get increased provincial participation in this area. He is convinced, it seems, that the job can be done just as well by some board which he intends to appoint in the interests of the whole country. I believe it is well known, however, that the interests of the whole country have not been well served up to the present time. This is why the party opposite me was turned down so resoundingly last year in every province but one. It is because hon. gentlemen opposite do not have a feeling for the whole country. They have a feeling for the triangle, Montreal-Toronto-Ottawa, and in this case I think it is Toronto which is calling the tune to which the government is dancing. I am not prepared to allow that type of interest to be injected into the national life of the country if I can possibly prevent it.
I should like to say something about the practical effects of this legislation. Here is a piece of legislation which will control every business and economic undertaking in the country right down to small businesses having $250,000 in assets and $3 million in turnover. Sometimes I think we become dazzled by figures. We must believe this is an awful lot of money and that these are large undertakings. I want to give hon. members an example of the kind of business these figures cover. I am thinking of the local Oldsmobile-Chevrolet-Cadillac dealership across from my office in the City of Drumheller. It employs a dozen people. It has assets of $150,000 and its turnover last year, in the second year of its operation under the present ownership, was $2 million. As things are going at present, it will not be long before its turnover exceeds $3 million in volume. Is it at all reasonable that a bunch of bureaucrats in Ottawa should be placed in the position of deciding whether or not it would be all right for someone from Montana to buy that business? What are we coming to when a government is so grasping that it wishes to exercise that kind of control?
I was about to mention that a rapeseed processing plant is presently proposed for the Town of Sexsmith in Alberta, a short distance from Grand Prairie. A report on this undertaking appears in the Albertan Business Report for November 13. I should like to quote from it:
This sleepy northwestern Alberta village where the main industry now consists of six grain elevators employing six people is about to get a shot in the arm from a $10.3 million rapeseed processing plant.
Sod for the plant, which will employ more than 60 people and have an annual pay roll of more than $450,000 will be turned shortly...

Nora Holscher, Village Secretary-Treasurer, says more than half the employees will come from Sexsmith, which has a population of 622, and the rest from the City of Grand Prairie, 12 miles to the south. "The plant will be the lifeblood of the village", Mrs. Holscher said.
The difficulty here is that money put up by Swedish and West German interests will finance the construction and operation of this new industry. What would happen if this development were proposed after the implementation of the legislation we are now discussing? There is a rapeseed crushing plant located in or close to the City of Montreal. Do you think, Mr. Speaker, that the bureaucrats would say it was of significant benefit to establish this new plant in Alberta when it might possibly have an adverse effect on employment in the City of Montreal? I wonder what the answer to that question would be.
I, for one, do not think it would be favourable to Alberta, especially in view of the fact that the minister wishes to retain political control over all these decisions. If he wishes to give us clear proof of his bona fides he would be advocating a screening office one step removed from his own office and not subject to his dictates. After all, he is going to appoint people who will do as he says. I think this screening board should be given a measure of independence and that there should be representation from all parts of the country among its members. As things are, perhaps there will be one member from the far west, one member from the Atlantic provinces and four or five from the centres of Ontario and Quebec, directing all the new investment which is to be allowed to flow into this country. I am not optimistic about how this thing will work, if it ever is allowed to work, which I hope will never be the case. As far as I am concerned, the minister has not shown his complete bona fides in the way he is handling the situation.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext: What about saying something positive now?

speechtext: Very well, I will say something positive. What this country needs is money to build. I would rather see Canadian money used before any other, but we will never develop this country completely by using our own financial resources. No other country has done so. The United States did not reach its present exalted position by building from within; it borrowed money extensively from Great Britain, France and other countries.

speechtext:
If the bon. member can tell me of any country that has been built up entirely by using its own resources, then I would be glad to hear from him. Indeed, I hope he is going to participate in this debate. If there is one country, I suppose it might be Saudi Arabia. We have great resources in this country, as I think all members of the House will agree, but they do not magically fall from trees. You do not gather them up with a rake. You have to build buildings and dig holes. Incidentally, I would remind the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orli-kow) that you do not dig for oil, you dig for coal. But he does not know too much about the industry.
The fact is that there is a lot of work to be done and it will take a lot of money. I completely agree we should use
November 21, 1973

Canadian money first, but when you have a coalition of socialists and semisocialists you are never going to have sufficient funds. All of the money will be wasted on grandiose, bureaucratic plans that take most of the thrust from the use of this money. The federal government itself is setting a bad example by paying higher and higher salaries. Look at our deputy ministers today. Certainly, they look after themselves very well. But you cannot have everything; you must have some sense of priority. If the federal government wastes money, then this sets a bad example to the provincial and municipal governments. They are just about as wasteful, but they have a good master to follow.
As I say, a lot of money will be required to develop this country. As Canadians, we should at least be given the same opportunity as foreigners to invest in our resources. This is what I have been requesting since I came here five years ago, but this bunch of so-called brains sitting on the treasury benches cannot seem to grasp the message that they should give Canadians a little bit of a break, or at least parity with foreigners, in the matter of investment. In this way you would be taking positive action. You say to Canadians: "We will give you a chance to invest in your country". But as long as we have something like the Benson tax bill that is going to take everything from our citizens or the great unemployment insurance rip-off, spawned by the hon. member for Verdun (Mr. Mackasey) and costing billions of dollars that could be better spent on developing the resources of this country, our citizens will never have sufficient investment funds.
Let me put on the record some figures that relate to the energy situation today. Over the next ten years, $1,000 billion will be required to be spent to find new sources of energy. The industry itself can put up about 60 per cent of that, or $600 billion. This leaves a shortfall of about $400 billion. What I am fearful of is that, far from having too much foreign investment in this country, we will soon be reaching the situation where we will not have enough money to develop our resources. In Canada alone during this period about $30 billion will be required. The industry will be able to supply between $20 billion to $25 billion from their own resources, though the amount can vary, of course, with government policy. This leaves a balance of $5 billion to $10 billion which must either be raised in Canada or brought to Canada from abroad in order to make sure that we have a secure supply of energy. Thank goodness the policies we have followed to date have provided a good source of energy supply. It is fortunate, as the hon. member for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay) pointed out, that federal government policies have ensured that this safe source of supply will be available to all Canadians. Nevertheless, we have to admit that shortsightedness is a human frailty which is found in all people, and I suppose in Canadians in particular.
I was disappointed to hear, in these days of shortage of supply, that when the province of Alberta offered to make sure that Canadian interests would be served first a spokesman for the province of Quebec said: "Well, if you insist on building a pipeline to supply us with the oil that we need, we might take it on the clear understanding that it is a two-way pipeline. Then, if circumstances change, we can send oil out west through this pipeline". I do not regard that as the type of statement that produces a great
Foreign Investment Review Act feeling of national unity in this country. I am happy, however, that the province from which I come has recognized its duty, as a partner in confederation, to ensure that Canadians from coast to coast will have oil and gas made available to them in this time of difficulty, even perhaps to the extent of damaging permanently the fields from which those resources come.
Whether or not the government is going to do anything along this line, we do not know. I have to admit that when such a proposal was first made in 1959 and 1961, the Conservative party was in office. Representatives of the Alberta petroleum industry came to Ottawa to see whether they would be permitted to supply their products to Montreal. At that time western oil was too expensive so the idea was dropped. Just four and a half years ago, in June of 1969, the offer was repeated, and again the door was slammed in the face of western oil interests. I think the offer was renewed in January of 1972, but a lack of interest was still shown. I hope that the opportunity will be given Albertans to assist their fellow citizens in this time of difficulty. However, the fact is that if we follow the line of thinking embodied in this bill we are not going to have sufficient known sources of supply in Canada, even though we know they are there. It seems that a number of people in the federal bureaucracy, the opinion makers in this country, think you can turn on oil and gas supplies the way you turn on the water faucet, but this is just not so. It takes a long time to discover reserves, and I am afraid that unless action is taken now to encourage exploration activity we will not have the known reserves required for the future.
At this time I should like to say something about the composition of the Canadian energy industry. This is a very technical and high risk industry requiring large amounts of risk capital. The industry is composed of over 600 different companies ranging in size from the major international companies with assets in the billions to one-man geological operations. In the past number of years there has been increasing development of Canadian-owned firms. This is really amazing when you consider the tax and other difficulties which have been placed in the way by this federal government. These small firms have been influential in generating a large body of expertise in all phases of this operation, but I am afraid this expertise will be lost as a result of the attitude of the present government. The development of this expertise has been inhibited to a large extent by our tax policies. Our policies do not encourage Canadian companies or individuals to carry out exploration for oil and gas in this country.
It is interesting to note that while we are happy to have our known reserves, we must recognize the fact that these are known reserves because the U.S. government has in its wisdom subsidized U.S. exploration to the extent of 90 per cent.

Mr. Speaker, I thank hon. members for the opportunity to continue, and I undertake not to impose on their goodwill for too long. I am afraid I have not progressed very quickly, as I still have a lot of material I should like to put on the record, but perhaps I might just finish this phase of my discussion.
It seems that recently there has been an increasing development of small independent operations in the oil exploration field in western Canada. Perhaps it would be useful to again look at some of the figures when dealing with this matter. In 1972 there was a total of 325 dry wells drilled in Alberta, of which there were 66 drilled by major companies. In addition 11 producing wells were drilled. It is interesting to note that you do not get a producing well

every time you put down a hole. During the same period of time, there were 259 dry wells drilled by independent oil companies, as well as 66 producers. Almost 81 per cent of the wells drilled in Alberta were drilled by small independent oil companies rather than by those major bogey-men my friends from Toronto seem to fear so much.
There was not the same degree of activity in Saskatchewan, but almost 92 per cent of the oil wells drilled there during the same period were drilled by small Canadian independent companies. The situation in British Columbia was somewhat different. The major companies seemed to have more confidence in the new government there, with the result that only 39.1 per cent of the wells drilled during that period were drilled by independent companies. At the same time all the wells drilled in Manitoba were drilled by independent companies. In total activity, 81.9 per cent of wells drilled in 1972 were drilled by small companies.
Considering the number of wells drilled one must realize that a great deal of money is required to carry out this activity. I am happy to see that Canadian companies are taking part to such a great extent in this activity, but I remind hon. members that they depend for their lifeblood on sources of funds outside Canada. These companies cannot operate without access to foreign investment. We must bear in mind that the financial communities of Montreal and Toronto are not free and easy with the money they control. An example of this is the fact that the premiers of various provinces, notably socialist premiers such as Premiers Barrett, Blakeney and Schreyer, immediately upon being elected ran off to New York, Switzerland and London for money. If there is so much money at such favourable terms in Canada why are these premiers not tapping this source? I know that members of the NDP will say that this is debt money rather than equity, but the fact is that the companies to which I have referred require debt money as well. That is the type of money we need in order to keep the cost of Canadian money competitive. There must be free access to foreign investment because Canadian investors have not shown any great ability to handle the job.

Mr. Speaker, a review of the progress of social, political, and economic thought since ancient times shows that interventionism evolves in spirals. This is the point I wish to deal with because I think that Bill C-132 relates to some kind of state intervention in very important areas.
We must accept this process not because we lack defensive means but because of our realism and understanding of the domestic and external economic and political environment of this country. If I were to give a name to this century, from an economic point of view, I would call it the "century of interventionism".
Interventionism is beneficial where it is well adapted. It is not surprising then to see states with the most liberal socio-economic ideas recognizing the principle of intervention and applying it in key areas of their society.
November 21, 1973

This is not the place to promote this principle but we should sensitize our leaders to this increasingly serious phenomenon in order to make everyone realize that this is not a magic panacea but rather a liberal principle that we should, in my opinion, not relinquish but modernize and adjust.
In liberal societies like ours, the intervention of governments is essential to regulate our activities. We must re-instate through government legislation the essential activities that will then become ordinary and timely.
The subject matter is very interesting and I could say, Mr. Speaker, that the present and former leaders of the government have implemented in the last years several interventionist plans in some very important fields. I could mention hospital insurance, the Canada Assistance Plan, unemployment insurance, family allowances, old age security, regional development incentives, social security, under which 50 per cent of all social security in Canada is paid by the federal government to the blind, the needy, the widows, the disabled, the welfare services and so on. Then the government intervenes in the areas essential to the quality of Canadian life.
Bill C-132 is merely intended to protect the high interests of the country and also to check in a certain way the economic problems caused by international operations.
Before dealing with the bill it could be useful to speak about the whole economic situation. Canada is a young country, a developing country, one of the largest territories in the world whose population is spread over 10 territorial entities and concentrated mostly in large centres.
Thus, the Canadian mosaic is characterized by population, geography, culture and economic voids. Political efforts consist, consequently, in rectifying the existing lack of balance between regions, areas, cities and urban centres, and also between fisheries and agriculture, between commerce and services, between communications and cultural laws governing the life style of Canadians.
The primary effort, I believe, should bear at first on the elimination of obstacles to development, while preparing welcoming structures to be used as solid foundations to the construction of a strong and united Canada.
The economic philosophy of the country and the noble nationalistic worries have left, in previous years, a free field to foreign societies and to capable businessmen, so that they were able to mold the Canadian economy in accordance with their own criteria.
As a matter of fact, during this stage of national construction and cultural harmonizing, Canadian leaders noticed that Canada's resources had passed into foreign hands, meaning that these resources were not used directly for Canadian needs, but in the interest of foreign countries.
Thus, Canada has become a raw material supplier, in the same way, maybe, as a few underdeveloped countries, which constitute a group of poor countries in front of the group of industrialized countries. The consequences of this situation on the Canadian economy are easy to forecast. Power no longer belongs to Canadians, but to those who
Foreign Investment Review Act own vital and economic interests, which causes a shift of the economic and political power.
Second, we have an economy sensitive to any sociopolitical change, hence the loss for all Canadians of the control over their social and economic destiny.
Third, the bridle of the Canadian economy is in the hands of foreigners and runs through the pulleys of foreign metropolises. I am talking here about multinational corporations.
In such a situation the effects of any economic chaos are easily felt because that close dependence ties us to economies enjoying far greater production and consumption capacities.
Fourth, the fact that Canadian products are destined to serve foreign interests results in a lack of jobs for Canadians. That is because those resources are channeled through a processing method without the Canadian economy, something which benefits in various respects to outside economies both in terms of employment, income, and market.
Fifth, that processing of resources moved outside our territory results in our infrastructure being incomplete and stopping at the limit of our frontiers.
The problems resulting from previous situations have the main effect of deteriorating exchange rates. Canada, a country rich in raw materials has to produce more, invest more, work more, and use more machinery to end up receiving in return the same service or the same machinery that cost increasingly more.
I could go on adding to that list, Mr. Speaker, but I think that the problem is well understood by the average Canadian citizen. We must now concentrate our priorities on curbing a situation unfair to Canadian interests.
This bill is undoubtedly a step in the right direction. It ensures a flexible Canadian attitude that I find wise and reasonable.
