speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, during this debate on third reading of this bill, we again are discussing the problem of foreign ownership of our economy and national life. It is too bad that, in respect of this bill, the minister did not see fit to accept some amendments, particularly the amendments dealing with the input the provincial governments should have with regard to the decision-making process of this tribunal which is being established. Without this possibility of the provincial governments having some input, the way the bill is set up makes it possible they would not even know that a takeover problem existed or that a company was being formed or being taken over until after the event. So, after listening to considerable debate, I am more than ever of the opinion that the effect of this legislation will not be what was intended because of its substantial deficiencies.
The first defect is that Canada should have expanded its approach to sector control of the economy, something which has already started in certain areas. But this legislation does not deal with that. In the beginning, I was of the opinion that there were certain significant areas of our
26635-77J

November 21, 1973
Foreign Investment Review Act economy that should have been protected from foreign ownership. We are involved in communications, yet sometimes when I listen to the CBC I wonder if it was worthwhile trying to protect that part of the economy from outside influences.
There were other areas, and I mention one, uranium. But it should be remembered that uranium is found in vast quantities around the world. We must also remind ouselves, when we are thinking of these things, that we have substantial stakes in other parts of the world. We have a large Canadian aluminum industry, and according to the papers the other day a survey indicates that the aluminum industry will probably grow much more rapidly than any other metal industry. But where does most of the raw material for that industry come from, Mr. Speaker? It comes from outside Canada. Would we be so happy if people in other countries insisted on that raw material being processed there before being exported?
But having decided on what I would call this second best course of controlling foreign investment, basically we are falling back on a tribunal of civil servants who will impose their will on each and every business, with the sanction of the cabinet. What more autocratic or more bureacratic decision making process could there be to decide on whether the person who wants to buy the corner store or the little gravel hauling industry is entitled to do so?
These civil servants live in Ottawa. One of the great failings of people who live in this atmosphere in the centre of the country is that they grow insensitive to the surrounding regions with which they are not familiar. This is a very understandable human trait. We all share it. But in a country like Canada civil servants living in Ottawa take the country to include an area 100 miles around Ottawa. They are conscious of the strong influences of Quebec and Ontario. As a result, I think the rest of the provinces are in for a pretty rough time at the hands of this tribunal. Perhaps we would have been more fortunate if we had had our national capital in Prince Edward Island, a small province, where it would not be subjected to such great pressures, from the larger provinces, economically and politically. But this is an idea I would not want to discuss at great length with P.E.I. members.
There has always been a large degree of foreign ownership of our economy. This has been due to the fact that we have wanted a high standard of living, and we failed to invest in our own country to the extent required. I suggest we have failed, not because we have not wanted to develop our country, but because we have not had the investment money to do so. Without foreign investment, we would be without jobs for our rapidly growing labour force. We must remember that each time we complain about high unemployment, the answer we get from the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) and the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro) is that Canada has the most rapidly growing labour force in the world. Without foreign investment, it would be impossible for us to give our people the high standard of living they demand. All of us want to live as well as the Americans, as well as the Europeans, and through our social services we are making a strong effort to do so. But it is interesting to note that the Americans, with whom we compare ourselves and who have a some-

what similar economy, have not developed the welfare state concept to the extent that we have, although their economy is considerably richer and more mature than ours and basically they could afford a much higher welfare state than we can afford.
Because oil and gas are so important at this period in our national life we should take a look at investment in this industry. We may not like the American companies, just as the NDP do not like them. We may be anti-American. We may deplore the fact that they are here. But, let us face it, without the American oil companies most of Canada would be pretty cold today, including B.C. and Ontario, because no oil of any consequence was found in western Canada before 1954 when the Leduc field was opened. I can remember my family living on a farm in which they invested $1,300 back in 1937, at a time when that was a lot of money, and all they got out of the Alberta oil fields was a little bit of paper. In the main the American investors drilled the holes. Those who tell the story of the finding of Leduc in 1954 can recount how the premier of Alberta at that time brought certain people down to Montreal and Toronto to see if eastern financiers were interested in investing in oil. The answer he got was, "So what? You have a hole in the ground with a little oil in it. We are not interested in investing in that." It is fair to say that probably they did not have enough money. They had other things in which to invest.
As a result the Americans took over the oil industry to a large extent, mainly because of their investing habits. It was not a question of the large oil companies in the beginning. Many small American individuals, the professional people, the lawyers and doctors, people who were willing to put $1,000, $5,000 or $10,000 into betting on a hole in the ground. It was just like betting at a race track. They were the ones who originally opened up the oil fields. And what did the American government do? It allowed these people to write off their investments against their personal income tax. Even yet, in the three western provinces where intensive drilling is carried on, most of it is done by small independent companies financed by similar types of American investors. It is only in the Arctic islands that the large oil companies are actually involved in drilling. After the holes are drilled, then the large oil companies take over.
In 1948 or 1949 a group of people in my town wanted me to join with them in an enterprise in which each put in a couple of thousand dollars to form a small oil company. In those days it took $10,000 to drill a hole in the Lloydmin-ster area. I did not get any results, so I suspended the operation. A year later I asked one individual if he was still involved in the Lloydminster oilfield. He replied that the federal government had changed the tax law so he could not now deduct his losses from his income tax, and he was not going to risk his money any further. It took 20 years for amendments to be made to the income tax law to provide that losses could be written off, and even then there was a maximum of $1,000 a year. So if you lost $5,000 it would take five years to write it off. Mr. Speaker, with inflation the way it is you should be able to write it off in six months if the amendment is to be of any value. This action by the federal government, however, does not seem
November 21, 1973

to have been any inducement for investment in the small oilwells.
Some people have said that the Maritimes and Montreal do not have any oil because of the Ottawa line. Perhaps the people in Ontario have paid slightly more to assure themselves of a supply of oil, but without this they would be pretty cold this winter. Until recently the attitude of the Americans has been that they did not want our oil, but after the Suez crisis in 1967 they saw Canada as a secure source of supply. For years the Venezuelans demanded that the Americans take a certain amount of oil from them but the Americans refused although at that time oil was a dime a barrel all over the world. One cannot help thinking that they would have been no worse off if they had dealt with the Venezuelans instead of the Canadians.
The Globe and Mail today carries a report to the effect that Mr. Bourassa is not enthusiastic about a pipeline to Montreal. He wants it if necessary apparently, but wants the federal government to pay for it. He also wants the federal government to pay for the oil that is transported through the line. According to the article he wants to continue to rely on offshore oil for the factories and refineries that he hopes to build in Quebec. I think this indicates the feeling that we will eventually return to normal conditions.
It has been said in this House by the Leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Lewis) that we will have to hold the line on gas and oil prices, and that after the end of January he will bring down the government unless this is done. I do not know how this fits in with the fact that Westcoast Transmission in British Columbia, encouraged by the B.C. Energy Commission, has raised the price of natural gas by 81 per cent. This fact was admitted by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald) in answer to a question I put to him a couple of days ago.
A report was carried on the radio last weekend to the effect that Premier Blakeney of Saskatchewan told the New Democratic Party convention there that the dwindling oil reserves in that province would last for about 16 years, but he added that if no exports were allowed the supply would last for 50 years. Does this mean that he intends to keep the oil at home, Mr. Speaker? Where would we be if we all adopted this attitude, that our resources must be kept within our provincial borders and not sold on the open markets of the country. There seems to be a great deal of inconsistency within the New Democratic Party.
If we deplore the foreign investment in our country, we should realize that there are many countries in a similar situation. In the last century the United States was largely financed by British capital. It is always stated that capital in the form of loans and bonds is better than capital in direct investment because of the possible conflict of interest between decisions made in local head offices and decisions made in corporate head offices outside Canada. I think this theory is greatly overrated because, although it is often indicated that decisions by parent companies outside Canada are not good for Canada, very little evidence of this has been produced that I have seen.
When this bill was in committee, the management of a small oil company with 28,000 U.S. shareholders was asked
Foreign Investment Review Act what influence the shareholders had on company policy. The management of this company was Canadian I might add. The answer given was that there was no evidence of influence, that all the shareholders wanted was a reasonable return on their money. They wanted some profit and the only time they were likely to interfere was if they did not get it.
There seems to be substantial evidence that we are buying back control of our economy. So long as the shares of large companies are traded freely on the stock exchanges, Canadian investors will be able to buy these companies back. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that many Canadians are not greatly interested in this. In effect, so-called Canadian ownership will depend largely on whether Canadians as a whole are interested in saving for this possibility. These savings in the final analysis are a matter of individual preference.
We have only to study the effect of the new Canada Pension Plan, which has a new cost of living clause built into it, to realize that for many Canadians in the lower income brackets it is almost foolhardy to have any personal savings. With complete medicine, hospital and nursing care for our citizens over 65 years of age, and with old age pensions and escalating Canada Pension Plan benefits, there is no need for the lower income Canadian to suffer. He may, of course, want to buy some article that will be helpful or gratifying in his daily life but in fact with the old age pension and the Canada Pension Plan available to him, the average individual could not save as much money as would give him a comparable annuity in his old age. Considering present inflation rates, why would any person want to save, say up to $500 per year, especially as the return on the money would be so small as to make the saving hardly worthwhile. I am reminded of the person who took an airplane trip to Hawaii; he said that at least the income tax man cannot take away that experience.
There is substantial evidence that investment money, at least from the United States, will recede in the immediate future. Passage of the American DISC program, the fact that there is a distinct possibility that Canadian provinces and municipalities may be shut out from the New York market, the surcharges of a year or so ago and changes in the investment picture all point to the fact that the Americans want their capital to come home. We had the funny experience of seeing Canadian unions trying to show their American counterparts the folly of supporting the Burke-Hartke bill presently before Congress.
The other day the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broadbent) was complaining that American auto companies had not invested enough money in auto plants on the Canadian side of the border. We are now witnessing the fact that at a time when the demand for oil and gas is at its height and we are running short of supplies, drilling is decreasing in the western provinces. It has decreased in B.C. and Saskatchewan. Last week, Winnipeg newspapers reported that Canadian expertise is flooding over into Montana. Apparently Canadian experts are active in all the oil fields of the world. Significantly, an analysist in a Montreal newspaper said the other day that if you want to invest in oils, invest in Canadian companies which are active outside Canada; do not invest in a company whose

November 21, 1973
Foreign Investment Review Act
main drilling rights are in Canada, because we do not know what their future will be.
Two or three years ago we passed legislation in this House aimed at controlling the manufacture of drugs in this country, in the interest of lower drug prices. That legislation wiped out their patent protection. It may have lowered drug prices. That is difficult to say. We are paying for that lack of protection in other ways. New drugs are being mentioned in the medical literature of the United States, of western Europe and of England. Those drugs do not seem to be available in Canada. I think, without any doubt, the drug legislation, which may have lowered drugs costs, has also discouraged the introduction of new drugs into Canada. The drug industry shows what foreign investment can do. Expertise in drugs is not confined to one country. Knowledge about drugs stretches beyond the borders of the United States, beyond the borders of western Europe, and extends to the communist world as well.
Turning to the instrument by which this government hopes to control foreign investment, its obvious weakness is its autocracy. Businesses will be controlled down to the value of $250,000. That means that a great many businesses will need to be screened, and often the seller will not know who the buyer is to be. In effect, this provision means that any business with three or more employees will have to be screened. I can see that the small businessmen will undergo considerable strain in trying to find out whether or not a buyer will come under the definition of foreign owner. I submit that the seller often will not know.
Let me refer to an article carried in the Globe and Mail of November 20, 1973, entitled, "Proposed investment review act comes under strong criticism." The investment review bill was strongly criticized by a former official of the department. The article reads in part:
The proposed federal Foreign Investment Review Act has come in for some strong criticism at the University of Toronto Faculty of Administrative Studies Issues at Interface Seminar.
Andrew Kniewasser, president of the Investment Dealers Association of Canada, said the difficulty with such legislation arises from the fact that 'its real effect will turn largely on the administrative performance of the agency.'
The act provided for creation of a review board reporting to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce with power to prohibit takeovers unless they are found to be of 'significant benefit to Canada.'
Mr. Kniewasser, a former deputy minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce said:
'I doubt very much if it would have been possible to limit administrative discretion by putting more criteria in the bill.'
In other words, the weakness of the bill is this: how are you to decide the criteria on which decisions should be based? You might as well toss a coin. You are as likely to be right as wrong.
The article continues:
Canada is still regarded by foreign investors as an interesting place to commit funds, with first rate economic propects and a rather moderate degree of government red tape . ..
If this bill passes, that may no longer be so. Mr. Kniewasser then said:
If the administration of the Foreign Investment Review Act does become restrictive or cumbersome or if it should lead to serious confrontations and additional uncertainties between the Government of Canada and the provincial governments, we would quickly be in trouble.
